Its volume depends mainly on the resonance of the bottle, and some instruments add a resonator box or a pickup. Because there is only one string the pitch is changed with the slide, unlike a multi-string guitar; it resembles slide guitar but is simpler in construction, and with a resonator box some versions come close to a single-string cigar-box guitar.

The diddley bow is an American single-string instrument, Hornbostel–Sachs 311.121.21, classed as a single-string zither. It usually stretches one steel wire between a board and two nails or screws, with a glass bottle under the string serving as bridge and helping resonance; the player plucks the string and moves a metal or glass slide up and down with the other hand to change pitch. It is traditionally found in the rural South of the United States and in African American communities, mostly as a children's or beginner's instrument, and today it also appears in solo and accompanying playing by professional musicians, and is connected with the slide technique of blues guitar.
迪德里一弦源自西非薩赫爾地區，如北尼日利亞與馬利，常由兒童以棍敲弦、另一人移動滑: The diddley bow comes from the Sahel region of West Africa, for example northern Nigeria and Mali, where children often strike the string with a stick while another person moves a slide to change pitch. It was developed by enslaved people in America into a children's toy, and researchers first recorded it in the rural South in the 1930s; traditionally it was regarded as a beginner's instrument, especially in African American communities of the Deep South. Many blues guitarists started on it but few continued as adults. Later came single-string cigar-box guitars with a resonator box, and electrified versions with pickups; Willie Joe Duncan's large electrified Unitar is one example. Professional players now also use it for solo and accompaniment.
迪德里一弦的聆聽場合主要在美國南方藍調與民間錄音中，可作獨奏或伴奏，也出現在藍調: The diddley bow is heard mainly in blues and folk recordings of the American South, as a solo or accompanying instrument, and also on recordings from blues and jazz festivals. Tracks such as Willie Joe Duncan's "Unitar Rock", One String Sam's "I Need $100" and Lonnie Pitchford's "One-String Boogie" let you hear its single-string plucking and slides. In recent years Cooper-Moore, Seasick Steve and Coco Elysses have played similar instruments, and a documentary shows Jack White building and playing one.

A glass bottle often serves as the bridge, both supporting the string and amplifying it. The other hand uses a metal or glass slide to change pitch. Some instruments add a resonator box under the bridge, close to a single-string cigar-box guitar, though the box material is not stated; recent electric versions carry a pickup, and the materials of the other parts are not described in the source.
